title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
summary: Formulates automated failure attribution for LLM multi-agent systems (which agent, which decisive step caused the failure) and releases Who&When, failure logs from 127 systems with agent/step annotations. Three LLM-judge attribution methods (all-at-once, step-by-step, binary search) reach at most 53.5% agent accuracy and 14.2% step accuracy.
relation_to_specdx: Shares the goal of localising where a run went wrong, but assumes the task and its checker are correct and always blames an agent step; SpecDx instead asks whether the failure belongs to the specification, using agreement across a population of interpreters rather than one trace.
baseline_notes: Run the three released Who&When methods (all-at-once, step-by-step, binary search; MIT code, OpenAI-style prompts that can be pointed at a local Ollama model) on each failing SpecDx run trajectory, with the task text T and the violated clause as context. Adaptation: add a third label so the judge can answer 'specification defect' besides naming an agent step, then aggregate per cell (a cell is flagged when most runs' decisive step lands on the same clause and the judge blames the spec). Gives a single-trace LLM-judge counterpart to SpecDx's population statistics; offline-capable with a local model.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
summary: Builds MAST, a 14-mode failure taxonomy for multi-agent LLM systems in three categories (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification), from expert analysis of 150 traces (kappa 0.88), and MAST-Data with 1600+ annotated traces over 7 frameworks. An LLM-as-a-judge annotator scales the labelling.
relation_to_specdx: MAST's 'system design / specification' failure modes (e.g. disobeying task or role specification) are agent-side labels; it does not ask whether the task specification or its checker is itself defective. SpecDx's defect taxonomy (contradiction, hidden requirement, ambiguity, weak check) is defined by satisfaction of the spec, not by agent behaviour.
baseline_notes: The released LLM annotator labels a trace with MAST modes. On SpecDx runs it would output agent-side modes; a run labelled with 'fail to ask for clarification' or 'task verification' failures concentrated on one cell could be read as an ambiguity or weak-check signal. Inputs: a full trace per run. Code is public (no licence file); needs an LLM endpoint, which can be local.

title: TRAIL: Trace Reasoning and Agentic Issue Localization
summary: Proposes a taxonomy of error types in agentic workflow traces (reasoning, system-execution and planning errors) and TRAIL, 148 human-annotated traces from single- and multi-agent systems on software engineering and information retrieval tasks. Long-context LLMs perform poorly at locating errors (best model about 11%).
relation_to_specdx: Localises errors inside one trace, including tool and environment errors, but treats the task as correct. SpecDx localises defects in the specification by contrasting many interpreters on the same cell.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
summary: Introduces Agent-as-a-Judge, where an agentic system with tools inspects another agent's workspace and trajectory and gives requirement-level feedback, and DevAI, 55 AI-development tasks with 365 hierarchical user requirements. The agent judge outperforms LLM-as-a-judge and approaches human reliability.
relation_to_specdx: Judges whether an agent satisfied each stated requirement, assuming the requirements are right; SpecDx inverts the question and asks which requirement or check is defective given many agents' behaviour.
baseline_notes: Point the released judge (MIT) at each SpecDx run's final DB state and trajectory with T split into requirements, and ask per requirement: satisfied / violated / requirement is unsatisfiable or ambiguous. Disagreement between the judge's verdict and the executable clause C on the same cell, across many runs, flags hidden-requirement or weak-check cells. Needs a tool-using LLM; can run offline on a local model with lower quality.

title: AI Agents That Matter
summary: Critiques agent benchmarking: a narrow focus on accuracy without cost, conflation of model-developer and downstream-developer needs, inadequate holdout sets that let agents take shortcuts, and poor standardisation that undermines reproducibility. Proposes cost-accuracy joint optimisation.
relation_to_specdx: Motivates treating agent benchmark results as noisy measurements; it does not diagnose defects inside individual task specifications, which is SpecDx's target.

title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation
summary: Presents the Holistic Agent Leaderboard: a standardised harness running parallel evaluations across hundreds of VMs, a three-way analysis of 21,730 rollouts over 9 models and 9 benchmarks (including customer service), and LLM-aided log inspection that surfaces unreported behaviours such as searching for the benchmark answers online. All logs are released.
relation_to_specdx: Provides multi-model rollouts on the same tasks, the raw material SpecDx needs, and uses LLM log inspection to find odd behaviour, but does not separate task defects from agent errors statistically. HAL's released logs (including tau-bench) could serve as an external population for SpecDx.
baseline_notes: Not a method; its released multi-model logs are a possible extra data source (repository archived).

title: $τ$-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
summary: Introduces tau-bench, retail and airline domains where an agent with API tools and policy documents talks to an LLM-simulated user, with evaluation by comparing the final database state against an annotated goal state. Proposes pass^k to measure reliability across repeated trials; GPT-4o solves under 50% of tasks and pass^8 is under 25% in retail.
relation_to_specdx: tau-bench is a direct instance of S = <T, C, Pi> (policy text, golden end state, scenarios) whose defects SpecDx targets; pass^k measures agent consistency but treats every repeated failure as the agent's, which is exactly the confound SpecDx separates.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs' Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
summary: ImpossibleBench creates impossible variants of LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench tasks by introducing direct conflicts between the natural-language specification and the unit tests; any pass implies a specification-violating shortcut, so the pass rate is a cheating rate. Used to study cheating behaviours, context engineering, and monitors.
relation_to_specdx: Its 'impossible' variants are seeded contradictions between T and C, the same construction as a SpecDx mutation operator for the contradiction type. ImpossibleBench measures agent propensity to exploit a known conflict; SpecDx must discover the conflict without knowing it is there, and agents that game the check are a threat to its signal.
baseline_notes: Not a detector; its spec-test conflict construction is a template for SpecDx contradiction mutants and its cheating transcripts a stress test.

title: Establishing Best Practices in Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)
summary: Shows that many agentic benchmarks have task-setup or reward-design flaws (e.g. SWE-bench Verified has insufficient tests; tau-bench counts empty responses as successes), which can mis-estimate performance by up to 100% relative, and proposes the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC); applying ABC to CVE-Bench cuts overestimation by 33%.
relation_to_specdx: Documents real weak-check and task-validity defects in tau-bench and SWE-bench and offers a manual checklist; SpecDx aims to find such defects automatically and per clause, with witnesses.
baseline_notes: A manual checklist; its items could be turned into an LLM static-review prompt for B1.

title: $τ^2$-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
summary: Introduces tau2-bench with a dual-control telecom domain (a Dec-POMDP where both user and agent act with tools), a compositional generator of verifiable tasks, a tool-constrained user simulator, and ablations that separate reasoning errors from communication and coordination errors.
relation_to_specdx: Target benchmark family for SpecDx; its later repair (tau2-Bench-Verified, amazon-agi/tau2-bench-verified) supplies real specification defects. tau2-bench attributes failures to agent reasoning versus coordination, never to the task specification.

title: AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in the LLM Agentic Systems?
summary: AgenTracer annotates failed multi-agent trajectories automatically by counterfactual replay (replace an agent action with a corrected one and re-simulate) and programmed fault injection, producing TracerTraj, and trains AgenTracer-8B with multi-granular RL. It beats large proprietary LLMs on Who&When by up to 18.18% and its feedback improves MetaGPT and MaAS by 4.8-14.2%.
relation_to_specdx: Counterfactual replay is an intervention-based test of a blame hypothesis, close in spirit to SpecDx's refutation by witness; but it presumes the task is solvable and the checker correct, so the earliest flipping correction is always an agent step. SpecDx asks whether any behaviour can satisfy C at all.
baseline_notes: No released code found in the paper's HTML; the replay idea could be re-implemented on SpecDx's executor but it would only ever label agent steps.

title: Aegis: Automated Error Generation and Attribution for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Aegis builds 9,533 multi-agent trajectories with labelled faulty agents and error modes by having an LLM manipulator inject context-aware errors into successful runs, and trains attribution models with SFT, RL and contrastive learning; fine-tuned small models rival much larger proprietary ones.
relation_to_specdx: Seeds errors into agent behaviour to obtain ground truth, analogous to SpecDx seeding defects into the specification with mutation operators; Aegis's seeded faults are agent errors only.

title: Where Did It All Go Wrong? A Hierarchical Look into Multi-Agent Error Attribution
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04886 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: ECHO improves agent/step error attribution in multi-agent traces over all-at-once, step-by-step and binary-search baselines by combining a hierarchical, position-based context representation, objective analysis by several specialised judge agents, and confidence-weighted consensus voting.
relation_to_specdx: Uses a committee of LLM analysts with consensus, like SpecDx's population, but the committee judges one trace for agent blame; SpecDx's committee members are executors whose disagreement is the evidence about the specification.

title: Spectrum-Based Failure Attribution for Multi-agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (FSE 2026)
summary: FAMAS is a spectrum-based failure attribution method for multi-agent systems: it replays a task many times, abstracts the trajectories, and scores each agent action's suspiciousness from how its activation co-varies with failure across the repeated executions, using a formula combining agent and action activation patterns. It beats 12 baselines on Who&When.
relation_to_specdx: Closest methodological neighbour in this theme: it localises blame from statistics over many stochastic executions rather than one trace, as SpecDx does. FAMAS still assumes the task and its oracle are correct and localises to agent actions, whereas SpecDx localises to specification cells and clauses, uses a latent-truth model with anchors rather than SBFL suspiciousness, and adds logical refutation.
baseline_notes: Can be re-implemented on SpecDx's run matrix: treat each (cell, observed value) or clause-violation event as a 'program element', each run as a test with pass/fail from C, and compute FAMAS/Ochiai-style suspiciousness. Cells with high suspiciousness and failure in nearly all runs across families would be flagged as spec defects. Needs: repeated runs with pass/fail and per-run event spectra (SpecDx already has these). No code repository located; formula is in the paper.

title: Abduct, Act, Predict: Scaffolding Causal Inference for Automated Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10401 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: A2P (Abduct-Act-Predict) scaffolds an LLM to infer a hidden root cause, propose a minimal corrective intervention, and predict whether the corrected trajectory would succeed, all in one pass, more than doubling step-level attribution accuracy on Who&When (47.46% and 29.31% on the two subsets).
relation_to_specdx: Simulated counterfactuals inside the LLM rather than executed ones; still blames agent steps. A useful prompt template if the 'intervention' is allowed to edit the specification instead of the agent's action.
baseline_notes: Released MIT code is a prompting scaffold over Who&When logs. Adaptation: feed a failing SpecDx run plus T and C, and allow the Act step to propose an edit to a clause or to T; if the predicted outcome flips only under a spec edit, label the cell a spec defect. Runs with any LLM endpoint including local Ollama.

title: RAFFLES: Reasoning-based Attribution of Faults for LLM Systems
venue: Proceedings of the 19th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
summary: RAFFLES is an offline, iterative evaluation architecture in which a central Judge proposes candidate faults and specialised Evaluators critique the faults and the Judge's rationale, applied to step-level fault finding on Who&When and on ReasonEval mathematical reasoning.
relation_to_specdx: Another LLM-judge attribution pipeline that assumes the task is valid; relevant only as an alternative single-trace judge baseline.

title: Where LLM Agents Fail and How They can Learn From Failures
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25370 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Introduces AgentErrorTaxonomy (memory, reflection, planning, action and system-level failure modes), AgentErrorBench with annotated failed trajectories from ALFWorld, GAIA and WebShop, and AgentDebug, which isolates the root-cause error and gives corrective feedback, improving all-correct accuracy by 24% and task success by up to 26% relative.
relation_to_specdx: A modular agent-error taxonomy for single-agent trajectories; the 'system-level' category is the nearest it comes to environment or task problems, and specification defects are out of scope.

title: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
summary: Proposes a reliability profile of twelve metrics along consistency, robustness, predictability and safety, grounded in safety-critical engineering, and evaluates 15 models on two benchmarks: accuracy gains have brought only small reliability gains, and agents remain inconsistent across runs and poorly calibrated.
relation_to_specdx: Treats run-to-run inconsistency as an agent property; SpecDx uses the same repeated-run variation, but decomposes it into agent error and specification-induced deviation.

title: DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: DoVer argues that log-only failure attribution yields untested hypotheses and that single-step attribution is often ill-posed because several distinct interventions can each repair a failure. It validates attribution hypotheses by targeted interventions (editing messages, altering plans) and re-execution, flipping 18-28% of failed GAIA/AssistantBench trials and validating or refuting 30-60% of hypotheses.
relation_to_specdx: Shares SpecDx's stance that a diagnosis must be tested by execution (validate or refute), but intervenes on agent messages, not on the specification; its finding that blame is not unique echoes SpecDx's set-valued truth.

title: Talk, Evaluate, Diagnose: User-aware Agent Evaluation with Automated Error Analysis
summary: TED evaluates conversational tool agents with expert and non-expert user personas, rewrites subgoals of existing datasets as natural-language grading notes scored by an LLM judge with new efficiency and progress metrics, and adds an automated error-analysis tool that mines inconsistencies between judge and agents to surface common errors.
relation_to_specdx: Its diagnosis step analyses judge-agent inconsistencies, a weak analogue of SpecDx's spec-as-fallible-rater anchor; but errors are attributed to agents, and grading notes are assumed correct.

title: Who Guards the Benchmarks? Automated Auditing of LLM Agent Benchmarks
venue: arXiv (camera-ready for COLM 2026 per arXiv comment; proceedings not yet confirmed)
summary: BenchGuard uses frontier LLMs to cross-verify all artifacts of execution-based agent benchmarks (instructions, environment, evaluation scripts, reference solutions) through structured protocols, optionally adding agent solutions or traces as evidence. It found 12 author-confirmed issues in ScienceAgentBench, including tasks made unsolvable by fatal errors, and matched 83.3% of expert-found issues on BIXBench Verified-50, at under USD 15 per 50 tasks.
relation_to_specdx: Same goal as SpecDx (find defects in the task specification and its checks, not agent errors) and also uses agent traces as evidence. It differs in method: a single strong LLM auditor reading artifacts, without a population model, typed satisfaction-based defect classes, clause-level localisation via MUS/MCS, or execution-backed witnesses.
baseline_notes: Strongest published counterpart to B1. Run BenchGuard's protocols on SpecDx specifications (T documents, tool descriptions, SQL checks, golden states), with and without SpecDx run traces attached, and score its findings against seeded mutants and real tau2-Bench-Verified defects. Code public (GitHub, licence NOASSERTION); needs a frontier LLM by default, a local model can be swapped in at lower quality.

title: Automated Benchmark Auditing for AI Agents and Large Language Models
summary: Auto Benchmark Audit (ABA) is an agentic framework that audits individual benchmark tasks for hidden environment dependencies, specification gaps, and limited grading logic. Over 168 benchmarks in nine domains it flags critical issues (ambiguous design, environment conflicts, incorrect ground truth) in over 25.7% of tasks; removing them shifts rankings and raises SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2 scores by about 9.9% and 9.6%.
relation_to_specdx: Directly targets specification and check defects in agent tasks, automatically, and validates against upstream fixes. ABA is a per-task LLM agent audit; SpecDx instead infers defects from the statistics of many fallible executors and confirms them with logical witnesses, and it types defects by satisfaction (contradiction, hidden requirement, ambiguity, weak check).
baseline_notes: Released agentic auditor and task annotations. Adapt by packaging each SpecDx scenario as a task directory (instructions = T, environment = DB + tools, grader = C) and running ABA; map its issue labels onto SpecDx's four defect types and compare precision/recall per cell. Needs an LLM agent backend; check whether it supports local models.

title: Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks
summary: Builds LLM scanners over agent transcripts to detect four validity issues (ground-truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, answer-format ambiguity), with human labelling rubrics, and evaluates them on held-out Inspect Evals benchmarks; the scanners found verified issues in five widely used benchmarks, though performance varied by benchmark, criterion and model.
relation_to_specdx: Uses agent transcripts, as SpecDx does, to surface benchmark-side problems, but scans transcripts one at a time with an LLM for predefined issue types; SpecDx aggregates across a population and localises to specification cells and clauses.
baseline_notes: Scanner prompts and evaluation code are released ('ABC inspired Scout scanners'). Adaptation: run the 'answer-format ambiguity' and 'tool failure' scanners over SpecDx run transcripts and aggregate per cell; serves as a transcript-level LLM baseline. LLM backend required.

title: Do Androids Dream of Breaking the Game? Systematically Auditing AI Agent Benchmarks with BenchJack
summary: Derives eight recurring benchmark flaw patterns from past reward-hacking incidents (an Agent-Eval Checklist) and builds BenchJack, which drives coding agents to synthesise exploits that pass a benchmark's checks without doing the task; on 10 agent benchmarks it reaches near-perfect scores on most without solving any task and surfaces 219 flaws, and an iterative patching loop cuts hackable tasks from near 100% to under 10% on four benchmarks.
relation_to_specdx: BenchJack's synthesised exploits are witnesses of weak checks (a wrong behaviour that passes every clause), the defect type SpecDx calls 'weak check'. SpecDx finds weak checks from the population plus symbolic search on the database; BenchJack finds them adversarially and does not address contradictions, hidden requirements or ambiguity.
baseline_notes: For the weak-check class only: point BenchJack at a SpecDx task with its checks C and let it search for a passing behaviour that violates T; a found exploit is a weak-check witness. Code public; requires a capable coding agent.

title: What Makes a Terminal-Bench Task Hard? Separating Genuine Hardness from Fake-Hardness on an Adjudicated Agentic Corpus
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26826 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Studies a frozen Terminal-Bench 3 production record (639 scored tasks, 28,801 trials) and asks what an all-fail task certifies. For 125 tasks with no honest pass, an ordered validity screen over reference-solution runs, empty-solution controls, adversarial trials, trajectories and telemetry keeps only 78 as certified-unsolved; the rest include broken oracles, infrastructure-dominated tasks, verifier bypasses and uncertified solvability.
relation_to_specdx: Squarely on SpecDx's question (a zero pass rate across many agents may be a task defect), using controls such as empty and reference solutions as witnesses. It is a task-level, partly manual screen; SpecDx is cell- and clause-level, statistical over the interpreter population, and types defects.
baseline_notes: The ordered validity screen (reference-solution run, empty-solution control, adversarial trial) is a useful procedural baseline: SpecDx's empty-behaviour and golden-state checks can replicate it, but no code is released.

title: How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28367 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Proposes a reliability framework for computer-use agent scoring (task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, reporting) and audits 150 failure-scored trajectories from five benchmarks: 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are wrong (10.7% evaluator false negatives, 4.7% broken tasks); genuine failures are then classified with a three-tier taxonomy.
relation_to_specdx: Quantifies how many agent 'failures' are really check or task defects, motivating SpecDx; the audit is manual.

title: ELT-Bench-Verified: Benchmark Quality Issues Underestimate AI Agent Capabilities
summary: Revisits ELT-Bench (data-pipeline construction agents) and shows capabilities were underestimated: an Auditor-Corrector method combining LLM-driven root-cause analysis of failures with human validation (Fleiss' kappa 0.85) finds that most failed transformation tasks contain benchmark-attributable errors (rigid evaluation scripts, ambiguous specifications, incorrect ground truth); ELT-Bench-Verified fixes them.
relation_to_specdx: A data-engineering, SQL-flavoured benchmark where failures are attributed to the benchmark rather than the agent, exactly SpecDx's dichotomy, with defect classes resembling SpecDx's (ambiguity, mis-keyed ground truth, over-strict checks). Its attribution is per-failure LLM RCA plus humans, not population statistics with logical witnesses.
baseline_notes: The Auditor step (LLM root-cause analysis of each failed run: agent error vs benchmark error) can be re-run on SpecDx's failing runs with T, C and the final DB diff as context; its per-run verdicts aggregated per cell give an RCA baseline. Benchmark code is public; check whether the auditor prompts are released.

title: SWE-Bench Pro Verified: A Reliable Benchmark for Software Engineering Agents
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08149 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Shows SWE-Bench Pro is undermined by reward hacking through leaked gold solutions or hidden evaluation information and by task-quality issues (misleading statements, improperly scoped tests), and releases SWE-Bench Pro Verified with anti-hacking safeguards and minimal task corrections; some models score substantially lower.
relation_to_specdx: Another curated set of real ambiguity and over/under-constrained-test defects in an agent benchmark; repairs are curated rather than inferred.

title: AgentSuite: Toward More Reliable Agent Evaluation with a Component-Based Benchmark Auditing Pipeline
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
summary: COBA decomposes each agent task into User, Environment, Ground Truth and Evaluation components and detects validity issues with hybrid rule-based detectors plus taxonomy-guided LLM evaluation. On six agent benchmarks it reaches F1 0.791-0.874 against experts, finds tau2-bench issues missed by manual verification, and ships in the AgentSuite platform with audited benchmark variants.
relation_to_specdx: The closest published competitor on SpecDx's own target (tau2-bench-style task specifications): automatic, component-localised flaw detection. It reads the artifacts with rules and an LLM rather than executing a population of interpreters, so it gives no satisfaction-based typing, no statistical separation from agent error, and no executed witnesses.
baseline_notes: Run COBA (released in AgentSuite) on SpecDx's tau2-style tasks and on seeded mutants; map its component-level issues (Ground Truth, Evaluation, User instruction) to SpecDx's cell/clause locations and defect types to compare recall and localisation. It needs an LLM for the taxonomy-guided step; rule detectors run offline.

title: Verifying the Verifiers: Failure Attribution for Agentic Benchmark Diagnostics and Training Data Curation
venue: ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Formalises failure attribution for coding-agent benchmarks as deciding whether a failure reflects an agent limitation or a task defect (ambiguous specification, flaky tests, broken environment), validates the taxonomy with human annotation (kappa 0.929), and presents AutoTriage, an agentic judge with sandbox access that executes code and tests; the best configuration reaches kappa 0.833 with humans, while weaker judges over-attribute agent failures to task defects.
relation_to_specdx: States SpecDx's exact dichotomy (agent error vs task defect) and automates it, threatening the novelty of the problem framing. It decides per failed trajectory with one strong judge and sandbox probes; SpecDx decides per specification cell from a population of executors, types the defect, and localises it to a clause or sentence of T. The reported pro-agent bias of weak judges is a useful warning for SpecDx's B1.
baseline_notes: Re-implementable: give an LLM agent sandbox access to the SpecDx PostgreSQL state and tools plus one failing run, ask 'agent error or task defect', aggregate verdicts per cell. No code release was found (workshop paper); the protocol is simple enough to re-create with a local model.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: A Validity Audit of Tool-Calling Evaluation
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02577 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Audits four tool-calling benchmark families (BFCL v4, tau2-Bench, LiveMCPBench, MCP-Atlas) on 496 expert-reviewed tasks and finds 18.5% evaluator-human misalignment: deterministic checkers show brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, incorrect ground truths and reward-basis misalignment, while LLM-judge benchmarks show rubric drift and large run-to-run variance (scores from 57.9% to 76.8% across 23 repeats). Releases a taxonomy, corrected evaluation components and the Tool-Veritas benchmark.
relation_to_specdx: Documents real hidden-requirement and weak-check defects in tau2-bench's golden-state checks, the class SpecDx targets, via expert review; SpecDx aims to find the same issues automatically from executor populations.
baseline_notes: Its released trace-level audit artifacts on tau2-Bench could serve as an external real-defect test set for SpecDx.

title: Faults in Our Formal Benchmarking: Dataset Defects and Evaluation Failures in Lean Theorem Proving
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
summary: Audits five Lean theorem-proving benchmarks with corpus-scale static checkers, surfacing 4,833 findings including 398 mechanically certified issues (counterexamples, vacuous theorems, unsound axioms), plus semantic defects where the formal statement does not faithfully encode the informal problem; shows defects both inflate and deflate prover scores and releases checkers and audit prompts.
relation_to_specdx: A formal-methods analogue of SpecDx: the checked statement (C) may not match the informal problem (T), and defects are certified by machine-checked witnesses. It relies on static checkers and prompts rather than a population of executors.

title: Finding Blind Spots in AppWorld and WorkArena Task Verifiers
venue: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development
summary: Audits execution-based task verifiers in AppWorld and WorkArena with source-informed mutation testing, finding blind spots such as duplicated non-idempotent writes that still pass AppWorld checks and incorrect persisted values that WorkArena checkers miss.
relation_to_specdx: Finds weak checks in database-state verifiers by mutating behaviours, the same 'wrong behaviour passes every clause' witness SpecDx's weak-check refutation produces; here the mutations are hand-designed from verifier source, not driven by an interpreter population.

title: Understanding Software Engineering Agents: A Study of Thought-Action-Result Trajectories
venue: 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)
summary: Large-scale empirical study of thought-action-result trajectories of RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover and OpenHands (120 trajectories, 2,822 LLM interactions) on program repair and issue resolution, combining quantitative analysis of action patterns and token use with qualitative assessment of reasoning coherence and feedback use, to characterise failure behaviour.
relation_to_specdx: Characterises agent-side failure behaviour of SE agents; it does not consider whether the issue or its tests are defective.

title: An Empirical Study on Failures in Automated Issue Solving
summary: Compares three state-of-the-art pipeline and agentic issue-solving tools on SWE-bench Verified and manually analyses 150 failed instances, deriving a failure taxonomy with 3 phases, 9 categories and 25 subcategories of failure modes.
relation_to_specdx: An agent-side failure taxonomy for SE agents; failures are attributed to tool behaviour rather than to task or test defects.

title: Understanding Code Agent Behaviour: An Empirical Study of Success and Failure Trajectories
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00197 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Analyses successful and failed SWE-bench trajectories of OpenHands, SWE-agent and Prometheus, finding that strategies such as defensive programming and context gathering drive success and that failed trajectories are longer and more variable, with failure patterns differing by agent.
relation_to_specdx: Observes that failure patterns are agent-specific, which is the 'scattered, interpreter-specific' signature SpecDx uses to recognise agent errors; no task-defect analysis.

title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09510 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Studies failure as a temporal process (onset, evolution, recovery) over 1,794 manually annotated Terminal-Bench trajectories from seven frontier models and three scaffolds, deriving 14 findings on how CLI coding-agent failures emerge and become unrecoverable.
relation_to_specdx: Agent-side process view of failure; complementary context only.

title: TrajAudit: Automated Failure Diagnosis for Agentic Coding Systems
summary: TrajAudit diagnoses failures in long, noisy trajectories of repository-level coding agents with an investigator agent supported by modules that reduce low-signal observations and track the causal chain of failure.
relation_to_specdx: LLM root-cause diagnosis of single coding-agent trajectories; does not consider the task specification or tests as a possible root cause.

title: Beyond Resolution Rates: Behavioral Drivers of Coding Agent Success and Failure
summary: Analyses 9,374 trajectories from 19 agents (8 frameworks, 14 LLMs) on the same 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks; finds that patch complexity does not explain difficulty (12 never-solved tasks need only simple patches) and that the trajectory-length/failure correlation reverses once task difficulty is controlled.
relation_to_specdx: Provides exactly the population-over-tasks matrix SpecDx exploits, and attributes all-agent failures on simple tasks to agent reasoning gaps; SpecDx would treat such consistent, cross-family failure as a candidate specification defect and test it.
baseline_notes: Its multi-agent trajectory corpus could be re-analysed with SpecDx's consensus signature.

title: UTBoost: Rigorous Evaluation of Coding Agents on SWE-Bench
venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
summary: Shows SWE-bench's issue tests are often insufficient so wrong patches pass, and proposes UTGenerator, an LLM test generator, and the UTBoost augmentation framework; it found 36 tasks with insufficient tests and 345 wrongly passed patches, changing 40.9% of SWE-bench Lite and 24.4% of Verified leaderboard entries.
relation_to_specdx: Detects weak checks (C looser than T) and repairs them with generated tests, using agents' wrongly accepted patches as witnesses; SpecDx detects the same class from interpreter populations on business specifications and certifies by witness states.

title: SWE-Bench+: Enhanced LLM Coding Benchmark
venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software
summary: Manually screens SWE-agent+GPT-4 'resolved' SWE-bench instances against the gold pull requests and finds that about a third of successful patches cheat via solutions leaked in the issue and many others pass only because tests are weak; builds a filtered SWE-Bench+ dataset.
relation_to_specdx: Real-world evidence of weak checks and leaky specifications in an agent benchmark, found manually; a source of real defect categories.

title: Are “Solved Issues” in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? An Empirical Study
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering
summary: Studies how many 'plausible' SWE-bench Verified patches from three issue-solving tools are actually incorrect, using PatchDiff, a differential testing technique that exposes behavioural differences between a generated patch and the developer patch, and inspects the discrepancies.
relation_to_specdx: Differential testing produces witnesses that a check is too weak (a passing behaviour that differs from intended), the analogue of SpecDx's weak-check refutation; it compares to a single reference patch rather than to the consensus of an interpreter population.

title: Seeing the Whole Elephant: A Benchmark for Failure Attribution in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
summary: Argues that Who&When-style benchmarks expose only agent outputs, and introduces TraceElephant with full execution traces (inputs and context) and reproducible environments; full traces improve attribution accuracy by up to 76% over partial observation.
relation_to_specdx: Reproducible environments allow re-execution, the precondition for SpecDx-style refutation; the benchmark still labels agent steps only.

title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?
summary: Who&When Pro is a large failure-attribution benchmark of 12,326 failed trajectories over 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks, built by exactly replaying a successful prefix and then injecting one failure so the golden label is known; analyses show systematic attribution patterns across modalities, protocols and model families.
relation_to_specdx: Uses controlled injection to obtain ground truth, as SpecDx does with specification mutants; the injected faults are agent errors and the task is assumed correct.

title: Rethinking Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark and Evaluation
summary: Argues that multi-agent failures often admit several plausible attributions and that single-root-cause benchmarks distort conclusions; proposes multi-perspective failure attribution, the MP-Bench benchmark and an evaluation protocol, and finds that earlier claims that LLMs cannot attribute failures stem largely from benchmark design.
relation_to_specdx: Accepts set-valued ground truth for blame, which parallels SpecDx's set-valued entailment sets A_c; still confined to agent-side attribution.

title: Conformal Agent Error Attribution
summary: Frames multi-agent error attribution with conformal prediction, giving finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees, with new filtration-based CP algorithms that predict contiguous step intervals in a trajectory; prediction sets are used to roll the system back and let it correct its own errors.
relation_to_specdx: One of few attribution works with finite-sample statistical guarantees, comparable in spirit to SpecDx's Hoeffding bounds; the guarantee is about locating an agent error step, not about separating spec defects from agent errors.

title: Causal Agent Replay: Counterfactual Attribution for LLM-Agent Failures
summary: Causal Agent Replay models an agent run as a structural causal model, applies do-interventions to steps and re-executes forward under the same stochastic policy to measure shifts in the outcome distribution; it provides a contrastive single-step estimator and a budgeted Monte-Carlo Shapley estimator with confidence intervals, validated on synthetic SCMs, and runs on hosted or local models.
relation_to_specdx: Distributional, executed counterfactuals with confidence intervals are close to SpecDx's sampling-based reasoning; but interventions target agent steps, not specification clauses, so a defective check would be misread as a pivotal agent step.
baseline_notes: Open source and supports free local models. Adaptation: on a SpecDx scenario, intervene on (a) the agent step that wrote a violating cell and (b) the clause in C (drop or relax it) and compare outcome shifts; a large effect only under clause intervention indicates a spec defect. Needs a re-executable environment, which SpecDx's PostgreSQL harness provides.

title: StepFinder: A Temporal Semantic Framework for Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2
summary: StepFinder is a lightweight failure-attribution framework that uses LLMs only to extract temporal semantic features of execution steps and then locates the root-cause step without full-trajectory LLM reasoning, reducing cost and noise from verbose logs.
relation_to_specdx: Peer-reviewed representative of efficient agent-step attribution; not concerned with specification defects.

title: Scope Delineation Before Localization: A Two-Stage Framework for Enhancing Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
summary: Proposes Scope Delineation Before Localization, a two-stage failure attribution framework that first identifies the failure scope (with stepwise or expertise-assisted strategies) and then pinpoints the failure step, improving Who&When step-level accuracy by up to 24.27%.
relation_to_specdx: Peer-reviewed Who&When follow-up; agent-side attribution only.

title: Towards Self-Improving Error Diagnosis in Multi-Agent Systems
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026
summary: ErrorProbe is a self-improving semantic failure-attribution framework that operationalises the MAS failure taxonomy to detect local anomalies, traces symptoms backward to prune context, and identifies the responsible agent and originating error step.
relation_to_specdx: Uses a failure taxonomy (MAST-like) operationally; agent-side only.

title: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026
summary: Surveys evaluation of LLM-based agents across core capabilities (planning, tool use), application benchmarks (web, SWE, conversational), generalist agents, benchmark dimensions, and developer frameworks, identifying gaps in cost-efficiency, safety, robustness and fine-grained, scalable evaluation.
relation_to_specdx: Background survey; benchmark validity and specification defects are not a focus, which supports SpecDx's gap claim.

title: Beyond Individual Intelligence: Surveying Collaboration, Failure Attribution, and Self-Evolution in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Survey of LLM multi-agent systems organised as the LIFE progression (capability foundation, collaboration, failure attribution, self-evolution), emphasising how errors propagate across agents and rounds and how attribution should feed self-improvement.
relation_to_specdx: Covers the failure-attribution literature as a stage of MAS development; it frames failures as agent or coordination errors.

title: EvilGenie: A Reward Hacking Benchmark
summary: EvilGenie is a reward-hacking benchmark built from LiveCodeBench problems in an environment where agents can easily hack (hardcode test cases, edit test files); hacking is measured with held-out tests, LLM judges and test-edit detection, and explicit reward hacking is observed in Codex and Claude Code.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that agents exploit checks when the task is hard; in SpecDx such exploitation would make a weak or contradictory check look satisfied, so gaming behaviour must be separated from faithful readings.

title: SpecBench: Measuring Reward Hacking in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
summary: SpecBench decomposes software tasks into a natural-language specification, visible validation tests that exercise features in isolation, and held-out tests that compose those features; the pass-rate gap between visible and held-out tests measures how far long-horizon coding agents optimise the tests instead of the specification.
relation_to_specdx: Makes the T-versus-C gap explicit: visible tests under-constrain the specification (a weak check by construction) and the held-out tests reveal it. SpecDx detects such under-constraining checks without held-out tests, from interpreter disagreement and witness search.

title: Is it Thinking or Cheating? Detecting Implicit Reward Hacking by Measuring Reasoning Effort
summary: TRACE detects implicit reward hacking by measuring reasoning effort: it truncates a model's chain of thought at increasing lengths and measures how early the reward is already obtained, since exploiting a loophole needs less effort than solving the task.
relation_to_specdx: A detector of check exploitation on the agent side; relevant to SpecDx only as a way to discount gaming runs before inferring specification defects.

title: AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
summary: AgentRewardBench has experts review web-agent trajectories from five benchmarks for success, side effects and repetitiveness, and evaluates 12 LLM judges against them: no judge excels everywhere, and the rule-based checks used by benchmarks tend to under-report success.
relation_to_specdx: Evidence that rule-based checks are often too strict (hidden requirements or mis-keyed checks rejecting valid behaviour), and that LLM judges are unreliable replacements; SpecDx diagnoses the check itself rather than replacing it with a judge.

title: AgentRx: Diagnosing AI Agent Failures from Execution Trajectories
venue: arXiv (accepted to EMNLP Findings 2026 per arXiv comment)
summary: Releases 170 manually annotated failed trajectories over 11 settings (structured API workflows, incident management, web/file tasks) with a critical step and a grounded-theory failure category, and AgentRx, which synthesises constraints, checks them step by step into an auditable log of violations with evidence, and lets an LLM judge localise the critical step; step localisation improves by 75% on average.
relation_to_specdx: Synthesises checkable constraints from the task and policy and records clause violations per step, much like SpecDx's per-run violated-clause sets; but it uses one trajectory and assumes the constraints are right, whereas SpecDx treats the clause set as fallible and aggregates violations across a population.
baseline_notes: Released by Microsoft. Run AgentRx on failing SpecDx runs to get the critical step and failure category; cells where AgentRx's critical step coincides across most runs and families are spec-defect candidates. Needs an LLM backend; constraint synthesis could be replaced by SpecDx's own clauses.

title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
summary: Proposes fully automatic weak-to-strong hardening of programmatic verifiers in agent environments: an isolated verifier sandbox plus a hacker-fixer loop in which agents search for exploits that earn full credit without doing the task and fixers patch the verifier.
relation_to_specdx: Automates the discovery and repair of weak checks via exploit witnesses, overlapping SpecDx's weak-check refutation; it does not address contradictions, hidden requirements or ambiguity and has no population statistics.

title: Characterizing Faults in Agentic AI: A Taxonomy of Types, Symptoms, and Root Causes
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06847 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))
summary: Empirical study of 385 faults sampled from 13,602 issues and pull requests in 40 agentic-AI repositories; grounded theory yields taxonomies of fault types, symptoms and root causes (34 fault types), linked by association-rule mining and validated with 145 practitioners.
relation_to_specdx: Software-engineering fault taxonomy of agent frameworks (implementation faults), distinct from specification defects in the tasks agents execute.
